result.summary: The Furies track Orestes to Athena's image and threaten him, then sing their binding hymn. Athena arrives, questions both sides, and hears Orestes' account of his father's murder and his own deed. Finding the case too grave to judge alone, she resolves to appoint sworn judges and found a lasting court.

scenes.title: The Furies track Orestes
scenes.summary: The Furies follow the blood-trail and find Orestes clinging to the goddess's image. They vow to drain him and drag him to the world below.
scenes.stakes: Orestes risks being hunted down and dragged living to the underworld for his mother's blood.

scenes.title: Orestes invokes Athena
scenes.summary: Orestes says he has been purified at Phoebus' hearth and calls on Athena to help him, wherever she may be.
scenes.stakes: Orestes needs deliverance from the Furies' pursuit.

scenes.title: The Furies' binding hymn
scenes.summary: The Furies declare their office and sing a spell to bind Orestes, claiming justice against the stained.
scenes.stakes: Orestes faces the withering of his life by their spell; the Furies fear losing their honour to Apollo.

scenes.title: Athena arrives and questions
scenes.summary: Athena comes from the Scamander, asks who the strangers are, and draws out the Furies' case, then asks Orestes to answer.
scenes.stakes: The Furies stand to lose their claim; Orestes to lose protection.

scenes.title: Orestes states his case
scenes.summary: Orestes says he is already purified, names his lineage, and tells of Agamemnon's murder and his own revenge urged by Loxias.

scenes.title: Athena founds the court
scenes.summary: Athena finds both courses dangerous and decides to appoint sworn judges for a permanent tribunal.
scenes.stakes: Athens faces pestilence if the Furies are wronged or if murder goes unjudged.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithets of Apollo, who purified Orestes and commanded the deed.
The Furies' name in the underworld.

notable_quotes.reason: Captures the Furies' belief that spilled kindred blood cannot be undone.
Athena insists on hearing both sides, a seed of fair trial.

analysis.text: Old vengeance-justice, embodied by the Furies, meets a new idea of reasoned judgment as Athena refuses to decide alone.
The scene prepares the founding myth of the Areopagus, Athens' homicide court, celebrating civic law over blood feud.

legacy.text: The founding of a jury court to end a blood cycle became a lasting image of law replacing vengeance in Western thought.

fun_facts.text: Aeschylus' Oresteia was first staged in 458 BC, and the Eumenides is its only surviving play to end in Athens.

language_notes.text: The 'voiceless informant' is the blood-trail, which reveals Orestes' path without speaking.
'Wingless flight' means the Furies traveled swiftly without wings, though they are winged elsewhere in the play; here it stresses speed over the sea.
'Aye' means 'yes' or 'indeed', here an exclamation of discovery.
'Fain' means willing or glad; 'fain to submit to trial' mocks his hope that sanctuary will let him be judged.
'Clouts of gore' are clots or shreds of blood; 'requital' means payment in kind.
'Meed' means due reward or deserved portion, here the punishment each sinner earns.
The 'Lord of Death' is Hades, ruler of the underworld, who was imagined as keeping a record of mortal deeds.
Purification by the blood of a sacrificed piglet was the ritual cleansing for bloodguilt, performed by Apollo (Phoebus) at Delphi.
Triton is a Libyan lake or river where Athena was said to have been born or raised; the Phlegraean plain is where the gods fought the Giants.
"A bloodless victim" means one whose blood the Furies will drain; he will be a wasted shade while still alive.
"Fatted and consecrate" treats Orestes as a sacrificial animal fattened and dedicated to the Furies.
"Span the thread" refers to Fate spinning each life's thread; the Furies' office was fixed at their birth.
"Sable-stoled" means dressed in black robes.
After the Trojan War the Achaeans gave Athena land near Troy as a prize; the Athenian claim to Sigeum is alluded to here, with Theseus' sons (Athenians) as its settlers.
Athena's aegis is her goat-skin mantle; she says its fluttering folds, not wings, carried her swiftly.
'Seen of gods' means seen by gods; she says the Furies resemble neither goddesses nor humans.
'Curses' is the Furies' name beneath the earth; in Greek, Arai. They are also called Erinyes.
'Bourne' means destination or boundary; she asks where the killer can end his flight.
The Furies mean Orestes will not swear the oath that would clear him, nor will he make them swear; 'fain' means willing.
Ixion, a Thessalian king, killed a kinsman and was purified by Zeus. Athena likens Orestes to him as a suppliant seeking cleansing.
Orestes came to Athena's statue as a suppliant, seeking protection. He claims he is already ritually cleansed of his mother's blood.
Greek custom held that a killer was polluted and barred from speech and company until purified, here by the blood of a young sacrificial pig.
Ilium is Troy; Troyland is the region around it. Athena aided the Greeks in its destruction.
The crafty snare is the net or robe Clytemnestra threw over Agamemnon in his bath before killing him.
Loxias is a title of Apollo as god of oracles. He commanded Orestes to avenge his father.
Devolved means passed down to her as her responsibility; stablish is an archaic form of establish.
Burghers are citizens of the town, here Athenians chosen as jurors.

context_notes.text: Orestes clings to the statue of Athena (the goddess's image) at her temple in Athens, seeking sanctuary after killing his mother Clytemnestra.
The Furies are ancient avenging spirits who punish kin-murder, especially the shedding of a mother's blood.
Athena is patron goddess of Athens, where Orestes has fled; she will later preside over his trial.
The Furies are daughters of Night, an ancient power older than the Olympian gods.
Leto's son is Apollo, who sent Orestes to kill his mother Clytemnestra and protects him.
The Furies are excluded from Olympian feasts and wear black, not the white robes of festivals.
The Scamander is a river near Troy. Athena comes from the Troad, where she has been claiming land granted after Troy's fall.
Zeus is the father of Athena; the Furies address her by this lineage.
Athena rejects the Furies' demand that Orestes simply take or refuse an oath, since an oath alone should not decide a case.
Orestes clings to Athena's image as a suppliant, a position that gave him religious protection.
The women are the Furies (Erinyes), goddesses who pursue murderers, especially kin-killers. Their anger threatens to blight the land if they are denied.
This is the traditional founding of the Areopagus, Athens' court for homicide cases, which Aeschylus' audience knew.

literary_notes.text: The Furies liken themselves to a hound tracking a wounded fawn, casting Orestes as helpless prey and them as relentless hunters.
Laughing at the smell of blood shows the Furies' grim, predatory nature and their pleasure in vengeance.
Blood as a 'flowing stream' lost to the earth conveys that a mother's death cannot be undone or atoned for easily.
Justice as a reckoning or account recurs here: the dead are 'held to account', echoing the play's theme of debt and payment.
Calling Orestes a fattened victim makes him their sacrificial animal, foreshadowing the feast on his living body.
This binding-song returns word for word as a refrain, giving it the force of an incantation.
Darkness, cloud and mist picture pollution as a gloom settling over the guilty man's house.
The Furies describe themselves as grim, despised and relentless, defining their role.
Athena is composed and fearless, feeling astonishment rather than fear, showing her authority and calm judgment.
The Furies' question presents matricide as beyond any possible compulsion, hardening their case.
Athena's insistence on hearing both sides prepares for the trial and the founding of court procedure.
Athena turns the Furies' claim to justice against them, saying they favour its appearance over its reality.
Orestes' epithet 'black-hearted' and his stress on the crafty snare paint Clytemnestra as treacherous and shape the court's view of her.
The balanced 'stay' versus 'drive them forth' lays out Athena's dilemma, with both choices ending in disaster.
Repeating 'a tribunal' stresses the new court's permanence and importance, anticipating Athens' civic institutions.
